solution_overview:
A factory inspects finished units for three defect types: Crack ($C$), Discoloration ($D$), and Warp ($W$). We are given the probabilities of individual defects, pairwise defects, and all three defects. These probabilities are modeled as subsets of a sample space using Venn diagrams or set theory.

We are given the following probabilities:
$P(C) = 0.18$
$P(D) = 0.22$
$P(W) = 0.15$
$P(C \cap D) = 0.06$
$P(C \cap W) = 0.05$
$P(D \cap W) = 0.04$
$P(C \cap D \cap W) = 0.015$
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

To find the probability that a unit has at least one defect, we use the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion for three events:

$$P(C \cup D \cup W) = P(C) + P(D) + P(W) - P(C \cap D) - P(C \cap W) - P(D \cap W) + P(C \cap D \cap W)$$

Substituting the given probabilities:

$$P(C \cup D \cup W) = 0.18 + 0.22 + 0.15 - 0.06 - 0.05 - 0.04 + 0.015$$

$$P(C \cup D \cup W) = 0.55 - 0.15 + 0.015 = 0.40 + 0.015 = 0.415$$

This means the probability of at least one defect is $41.5\%$. The claim states this probability is above $43\%$, which is false, so the statement is False.

**B.** → False

The probability of exactly one defect type can be found by summing the probabilities of each defect occurring alone, which is given by the formula:

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = P(C) + P(D) + P(W) - 2P(C \cap D) - 2P(C \cap W) - 2P(D \cap W) + 3P(C \cap D \cap W)$$

Substituting the given probabilities:

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.18 + 0.22 + 0.15 - 2(0.06) - 2(0.05) - 2(0.04) + 3(0.015)$$

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.55 - 0.12 - 0.10 - 0.08 + 0.045$$

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.25 + 0.045 = 0.295$$

This means the probability of exactly one defect is $29.5\%$. The claim states this probability exceeds $30\%$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The probability of exactly two defect types can be found using the formula:

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = P(C \cap D) + P(C \cap W) + P(D \cap W) - 3P(C \cap D \cap W)$$

Substituting the given probabilities:

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.06 + 0.05 + 0.04 - 3(0.015)$$

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.15 - 0.045 = 0.105$$

This means the probability of exactly two defect types is $10.5\%$. The claim states this probability is at least $10\%$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The probability that the unit has no defects is the complement of having at least one defect. We calculated the probability of at least one defect in statement A.

$$P(\text{no defects}) = 1 - P(C \cup D \cup W)$$

Using the result from statement A:

$$P(\text{no defects}) = 1 - 0.415$$

$$P(\text{no defects}) = 0.585$$

This means the probability of no defects is $58.5\%$. The claim states this probability is under $58\%$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The probability that the unit has at least two defect types is the sum of the probability of exactly two defects and the probability of exactly three defects.

$$P(\text{at least two}) = P(\text{exactly two}) + P(C \cap D \cap W)$$

Using the result for $P(\text{exactly two})$ from statement C and the given $P(C \cap D \cap W)$:

$$P(\text{at least two}) = 0.105 + 0.015$$

$$P(\text{at least two}) = 0.120$$

This means the probability of at least two defect types is $12.0\%$. The claim states this probability is under $13\%$, so the statement is True.
